structures.name: frontal lobe
structures.definition: The largest lobe of each hemisphere, in front of the central sulcus.
structures.function: Plans and controls movement, makes decisions, holds attention and regulates behaviour and personality.
structures.why: Its size reflects how much of human behaviour depends on planning and self-control.

notes.nursing: Damage can cause disinhibition and personality change; family reports of “not himself” matter.
notes.medicine: Phineas Gage is the classic case of frontal injury changing personality.

structures.name: precentral gyrus
structures.definition: Strip of cortex running from top to side of each hemisphere just in front of the central sulcus.
structures.function: Sends the commands that move the opposite side of the body.
structures.why: The body is mapped along it (the motor homunculus), with large areas for the hand and face.

notes.medicine: A stroke here causes weakness on the opposite side; the leg area lies on the medial surface.
notes.physio: Rehabilitation after stroke relies on neighbouring cortex taking over its lost areas.

structures.name: inferior frontal gyrus
structures.definition: Lowest of the three horizontal folds on the side of the frontal lobe.
structures.function: On the dominant side (usually left) it contains Broca’s area, which produces speech.
structures.why: Speech production sits next to the motor areas for the mouth and larynx.

notes.medicine: Damage gives expressive (Broca’s) aphasia: slow, effortful speech with good understanding.
notes.nursing: Patients with expressive aphasia often understand; use yes/no questions and give them time.

structures.name: parietal lobe
structures.definition: Lobe behind the central sulcus and above the lateral sulcus.
structures.function: Processes touch and body position and builds the sense of where things are in space.
structures.why: It combines senses into a map of the body and its surroundings.

notes.medicine: Right-sided damage can cause neglect of the left side of space.
notes.nursing: Patients with neglect may ignore food on one side of the plate; approach from the unaffected side.

structures.name: postcentral gyrus
structures.definition: Strip of cortex just behind the central sulcus.
structures.function: Receives touch, pain and position sense from the opposite side of the body.
structures.why: The body is mapped along it (the sensory homunculus), with large areas for lips and fingertips.

notes.medicine: A lesion causes loss of fine sensation on the opposite side.

structures.name: temporal lobe
structures.definition: Lobe below the lateral sulcus, behind the temple.
structures.function: Processes hearing, language comprehension and recognition of objects and faces, and helps form memories.
structures.why: Lying near the ear, it handles sound; its inner parts link to the memory system.

notes.medicine: Wernicke’s area (comprehension) is in the back of its superior gyrus on the dominant side.
notes.nursing: Temporal lobe seizures may present as déjà vu, odd smells or lip-smacking rather than convulsions.

structures.name: occipital lobe
structures.definition: Lobe at the back of each hemisphere, resting on the tentorium.
structures.function: Contains the primary visual cortex, which receives and interprets what the eyes see.
structures.why: Vision needs a large area of cortex, placed at the back where the visual pathways end.

notes.medicine: A stroke of one side causes loss of the opposite half of the visual field (homonymous hemianopia).
notes.sports: A blow to the back of the head can cause visual disturbance after concussion.

structures.name: insula
structures.definition: Lobe of cortex hidden deep in the lateral sulcus, covered by the frontal, parietal and temporal lobes.
structures.function: Senses the body’s internal state (heartbeat, gut, pain) and contributes to taste and emotion.
structures.why: It turns signals from inside the body into feelings such as disgust or breathlessness.

notes.medicine: Middle cerebral artery strokes often involve it.

structures.name: cingulate gyrus
structures.definition: Curved fold on the inner surface of each hemisphere, wrapping above the large band of fibres joining the hemispheres.
structures.function: Links emotion, motivation and attention, and helps detect errors and pain.
structures.why: Part of the limbic system, it connects feelings with behaviour.

notes.medicine: Under raised pressure it can herniate under the falx (subfalcine herniation).

structures.name: corpus callosum
structures.definition: The largest band of white-matter fibres, joining the two cerebral hemispheres.
structures.function: Lets the two hemispheres share information.
structures.why: Each hemisphere controls the opposite body side, so they must communicate constantly.

notes.medicine: Cutting it (callosotomy) for epilepsy can cause “split-brain” effects.

structures.name: thalamus
structures.definition: Paired egg-shaped mass of grey matter at the centre of the brain, either side of the third ventricle.
structures.function: Relays and filters sensory and motor signals on their way to the cortex.
structures.why: Almost every sense (except smell) is checked here before reaching awareness.

notes.medicine: Thalamic strokes can cause severe pain on the opposite side (thalamic pain syndrome).

structures.name: hypothalamus
structures.definition: Small region below the thalamus, forming the floor of the third ventricle.
structures.function: Controls temperature, hunger, thirst, sleep cycles and the pituitary gland.
structures.why: It keeps the body’s internal conditions stable, linking the nervous and hormonal systems.

notes.nursing: Damage can cause wild temperature swings and diabetes insipidus (large volumes of dilute urine).

structures.name: hippocampus
structures.definition: Curved ridge of grey matter in the floor of the temporal horn of the lateral ventricle.
structures.function: Forms new memories of facts and events and maps space.
structures.why: It binds experiences together so they can be stored elsewhere in the cortex.

notes.medicine: One of the first areas damaged in Alzheimer’s disease; very sensitive to lack of oxygen.
notes.nursing: New memories are lost first in dementia; old memories are often preserved.

structures.name: amygdala
structures.definition: Almond-shaped cluster of nuclei deep in the front of the temporal lobe.
structures.function: Detects threats and drives fear, and attaches emotional weight to memories.
structures.why: Fast threat detection, before conscious thought, helped survival.

notes.medicine: Overactivity is implicated in anxiety disorders and PTSD.

structures.name: caudate nucleus
structures.definition: C-shaped nucleus curving along the wall of the lateral ventricle.
structures.function: Part of the basal nuclei: helps select and start movements and supports learning.
structures.why: Its loop with the cortex filters which actions go ahead.

notes.medicine: Wastes early in Huntington’s disease, widening the lateral ventricles on scans.

structures.name: putamen
structures.definition: Rounded nucleus lying outside the internal capsule, forming the outer part of the lentiform nucleus.
structures.function: Regulates movement and motor learning as part of the basal nuclei.
structures.why: It turns learned movements into smooth automatic routines.

notes.medicine: The commonest site of hypertensive intracerebral haemorrhage.

structures.name: globus pallidus
structures.definition: Pale wedge-shaped nucleus lying inside the putamen, forming the inner lentiform nucleus.
structures.function: The main output of the basal nuclei, braking unwanted movement.
structures.why: Its constant inhibition keeps movements from starting unless they are selected.

notes.medicine: A target for deep brain stimulation in Parkinson’s disease and dystonia.

structures.name: internal capsule
structures.definition: V-shaped band of white matter between the thalamus, caudate and lentiform nuclei.
structures.function: Carries motor and sensory fibres between the cortex and the brainstem and spinal cord.
structures.why: All the main highways to and from the cortex funnel through it.

notes.medicine: A small stroke here causes dense weakness of the whole opposite side (pure motor stroke).

structures.name: cerebellum
structures.definition: Rounded, finely folded structure behind the brainstem, under the occipital lobes.
structures.function: Coordinates movement, balance and posture and fine-tunes timing.
structures.why: It compares intended movement with actual movement and corrects errors.

notes.nursing: Cerebellar signs: unsteady gait, slurred speech, tremor on reaching; alcohol affects it early.
notes.physio: Balance and coordination training help after cerebellar stroke.
notes.medicine: Damage affects the same side of the body.

structures.name: midbrain
structures.definition: Top part of the brainstem, between the thalamus and the pons.
structures.function: Controls eye movements and pupil reflexes and relays hearing and vision signals.
structures.why: It holds reflex centres that turn the eyes and head toward sights and sounds.

notes.medicine: Contains the substantia nigra, which degenerates in Parkinson’s disease.
notes.nursing: Fixed, dilated pupils on a neuro check can signal pressure on the midbrain.

structures.name: pons
structures.definition: Bulging middle part of the brainstem, in front of the cerebellum.
structures.function: Relays signals to the cerebellum and helps control breathing, sleep and facial movement.
structures.why: Its bulk is the bridge of fibres carrying cortex signals to the cerebellum.

notes.medicine: Cranial nerves V–VIII arise around it; a pontine stroke can cause locked-in syndrome.

structures.name: medulla oblongata
structures.definition: Lowest part of the brainstem, continuous with the spinal cord at the foramen magnum.
structures.function: Controls breathing, heart rate, blood pressure, swallowing and vomiting.
structures.why: The vital reflexes that keep us alive run here, below conscious control.

notes.medicine: Coning (tonsillar herniation) compresses it, causing respiratory arrest.
notes.nursing: Rising blood pressure with slowing pulse and irregular breathing (Cushing’s triad) is a late sign of raised pressure.

structures.name: lateral ventricles
structures.definition: Pair of C-shaped fluid-filled cavities, one in each cerebral hemisphere.
structures.function: Produce cerebrospinal fluid (from choroid plexus) and pass it to the third ventricle.
structures.why: Fluid cushions the brain and carries away waste.

notes.medicine: They enlarge in hydrocephalus; a drain may be placed in one to relieve pressure.
notes.nursing: Check external ventricular drain height and output hourly.

structures.name: third ventricle
structures.definition: Narrow midline fluid space between the two thalami.
structures.function: Passes cerebrospinal fluid from the lateral ventricles to the cerebral aqueduct.
structures.why: A central channel links the fluid spaces of both hemispheres to the brainstem.

notes.medicine: A colloid cyst can block its entrance and cause sudden hydrocephalus.

structures.name: fourth ventricle
structures.definition: Diamond-shaped fluid space between the brainstem and the cerebellum.
structures.function: Lets cerebrospinal fluid escape into the space around the brain and spinal cord.
structures.why: Its openings are the main exit from the internal fluid system.

notes.medicine: Blockage of its outlets causes obstructive hydrocephalus.

structures.name: optic chiasm
structures.definition: X-shaped crossing of the visual fibres just above the pituitary gland.
structures.function: Sends fibres from the inner half of each retina to the opposite side of the brain.
structures.why: Crossing lets each hemisphere see the opposite half of the visual world with both eyes.

notes.medicine: A pituitary tumour pressing on it causes loss of both outer visual fields (bitemporal hemianopia).

structures.name: optic nerve
structures.definition: Nerve running from the back of each eye to the crossing of visual fibres above the pituitary.
structures.function: Carries visual information from the retina to the brain.
structures.why: Each eye has its own cable carrying about a million fibres.

notes.medicine: Swelling of its head (papilloedema) on fundoscopy is a sign of raised intracranial pressure.
notes.nursing: Pupil reactions test it together with the oculomotor nerve.

structures.name: pituitary gland
structures.definition: Pea-sized gland hanging from the base of the brain in a saddle of the sphenoid bone.
structures.function: Releases hormones controlling growth, the thyroid, adrenals, reproduction, milk and water balance.
structures.why: It translates signals from the hypothalamus into hormones for the whole body.

notes.medicine: Tumours can cause hormone excess (e.g. acromegaly) and visual field loss.
notes.nursing: After pituitary surgery, measure urine output: diabetes insipidus is common.

structures.name: pineal gland
structures.definition: Tiny pine-cone-shaped gland at the back of the third ventricle.
structures.function: Secretes melatonin, which helps set the sleep–wake cycle.
structures.why: It turns information about darkness into a hormonal signal of night.

notes.medicine: Often calcifies with age and shows up as a midline marker on X-ray and CT.

structures.name: fornix
structures.definition: Arched bundle of fibres running from the hippocampus over the thalamus to the mammillary bodies.
structures.function: Carries output from the hippocampus as part of the memory circuit.
structures.why: It links the memory-forming hippocampus to the rest of the limbic system.

notes.medicine: Damage (e.g. after surgery for a colloid cyst) can cause memory loss.

structures.name: mammillary bodies
structures.definition: Two small round bumps on the underside of the brain behind the pituitary stalk.
structures.function: Relay memory signals from the hippocampus toward the thalamus.
structures.why: They are a waypoint in the circuit that consolidates new memories.

notes.medicine: Damaged in thiamine deficiency (Wernicke–Korsakoff syndrome).
notes.nursing: Give thiamine before glucose in patients with alcohol dependence.
